Lessons.Title: Interpret Division Expressions
ExplanationParagraphs: Division means putting a total into equal groups. The divisor can identify HOW MANY groups are already given or HOW MANY items belong in each group. The same expression may represent two different stories; the mathematical quotient alone does not identify the story's unknown.

Warm-up — Number Talk: More or Less? (10 min): 500−475=25, 504−475=29, 512−475=37 and 512−449=63. Use mental subtraction and notice that raising the starting value increases the difference; decreasing the number subtracted also increases it.

Activity1 — Spinning Tops (10 min): match five source situations to the expression choices: Clare’s four equal colour sets from24→24÷4 (source C); two painters sharing24→24÷2 (A); 24 in six equal boxes→24÷6 (E); 12 gifts at two per person→12÷2 (B); and 12 shared by six friends→12÷6 (D). Explain why the divisor names the known group quantity in every story.

Activity2 — Cars in Boxes (10 min): Han has21 toy cars. Three BOXES of equal size requires21÷3=7 cars per box. THREE CARS in each box also requires21÷3=7, but now seven is the count of boxes. The divisor has two different meanings; teach both explicitly and preserve the bilingual MLR2 collection of precise terms.

Activity3 — Stacks of Blocks (15 min): source diagram A shows2 stacks of3, and B shows3 stacks of2. The original expressions C=6÷2 and D=6÷3. Kiran (two blocks in each stack)→B,C; Han (two equal stacks)→A,C; Jada (three per stack)→A,D; Mai (three equal stacks)→B,D. These are not four interchangeable drawings; context controls which is correct.

Lesson synthesis (10 min): explain that the same expression can refer to different division types, while the same finished drawing can correspond to different expressions when the divisor describes a different known quantity. A teacher evaluates sketches, written justifications, partner reasoning and precise units.

Original source is the 2021 first edition, not the independently authored Edulytics exit task. Original photos (some third-party) are not copied; original student PDF pixels and gated Han’s Tops publisher Cool-down remain outside verified scope. Stage D and tests have not run.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unknown group size
KeyConcepts.Definition: Total and group count are known.
KeyConcepts.Rule: group size = total ÷ known group count

KeyConcepts.Title: Unknown group count
KeyConcepts.Definition: Total and group size are known.
KeyConcepts.Rule: group count = total ÷ known group size

KeyConcepts.Title: The divisor
KeyConcepts.Definition: The quantity by which a total is divided; the story establishes its meaning.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The divisor is not automatically the group count.
KeyConcepts.Example: 21÷3 means both Han stories; interpretation changes

KeyConcepts.Title: Story and drawing
KeyConcepts.Definition: A group diagram identifies the number of groups and items per group.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check both representation and division expression against the question.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two stacks of3 can be described by6÷2 or6÷3 depending on question

WorkedExamples.Title: Five spinning-top expression matches
WorkedExamples.Question: Which original expressions match five original contexts?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify total and known grouping quantity.
Steps: Diego two gifts per friend:12÷2=6, B.
WorkedExamples.Check: Re-multiply group count by group size for all five.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two interpretations of 21÷3
WorkedExamples.Question: Does21÷3 represent three boxes or three cars per box?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the context to define the divisor.
Steps: Three boxes given: seven cars PER box.
Three cars per box given: seven BOXES.
Answer units and picture differ despite the same numerical quotient.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both original situations;7 per box OR7 boxes.
WorkedExamples.Check: 3×7=21 in both arrangements; identify the unknown separately.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four block matches
WorkedExamples.Question: Match six-block stories to diagrams A/B and expressions C/D.
WorkedExamples.Method: Diagram A=2×3; B=3×2. Expression C=6÷2; D=6÷3.
Steps: Kiran two per stack→3 stacks; source B/C.
Han two stacks→3 per stack; source A/C.
Jada three per stack→2 stacks; source A/D.
Mai three stacks→2 per stack; source B/D.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Kiran B/C; Han A/C; Jada A/D; Mai B/D.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each picture holds six; group count and group size are consistent.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Always read the divisor as the number of groups.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: For the store,6 is known box count; for Diego,2 is a known number of tops per friend.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State what the divisor describes in this specific story.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Only select the correct numerical result, not the correct source diagram.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Kiran and Han both use6÷2 but need different drawings.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Validate group count and group size against the story.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume drawing A automatically means expression C.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Han uses A/C; Jada uses A/D, so the drawing alone does not identify which given number is divisor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Refer to the original context for the unknown quantity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Read 512−449 as the same difference as 512−475.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The subtrahend decreases by26, so the difference rises by26 from37 to63.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the numbers being subtracted as well as the starting value.

SummaryPoints: Spinning Tops five expression letters C,A,E,B,D in source story order.
Two Han21÷3 situations both have quotient7 but different units.
Block drawing A=2 groups3, B=3 groups2; Kiran B/C, Han A/C, Jada A/D, Mai B/D.
